{{Short description|Mathematics, group theory}}
{{For|the counting result sometimes called "Burnside's theorem"|Burnside's lemma}}
[[Image:Burnside 2.jpeg|thumb|William Burnside.]]
In [[mathematics]], '''Burnside's theorem''' in [[group theory]] states that if <math>G</math> is a [[finite group]] of [[Order (group theory)|order]] <math>p^a q^b</math> where <math>p</math> and <math>q</math> are [[prime number]]s, and <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> are [[negative and positive numbers|non-negative]] [[integer]]s, then <math>G</math> is [[Solvable group|solvable]]. Hence each non-Abelian [[finite simple group]] has order divisible by at least three distinct primes.

==History==
The theorem was proved by {{harvs|txt|authorlink=William Burnside|first=William |last=Burnside|year=1904}} using the [[representation theory of finite groups]]. Several special cases of the theorem had previously been proved by Burnside in 1897, [[Camille Jordan|Jordan]] in 1898, and [[Ferdinand Georg Frobenius|Frobenius]] in 1902. [[John G. Thompson]] pointed out that a proof avoiding the use of representation theory could be extracted from his work in the 1960s and 1970s on the [[N-group (finite group theory)|N-group theorem]], and this was done explicitly by {{harvtxt|Goldschmidt|1970}} for groups of odd order, and by {{harvtxt|Bender|1972}} for groups of even order. {{harvtxt|Matsuyama|1973}} simplified the proofs.

==Proof==
The following proof — using more background than Burnside's — is by [[Proof by contradiction|contradiction]]. Let <math>p^a q^b</math> be the smallest product of two prime powers, such that there is a non-solvable group <math>G</math> whose order is equal to this number.
:*<math>G</math> '''is a [[simple group]] with trivial [[Center (group theory)|center]] and''' <math>a</math> '''is not zero.'''
If <math>G</math> had a [[Trivial group|nontrivial]] proper [[normal subgroup]] <math>H</math>, then (because of the minimality of ''<math>G</math>''), <math>H</math> and <math>G / H</math> would be solvable, so <math>G</math> as well, which would contradict our assumption. So <math>G</math> is simple.

If <math>a</math> were zero, <math>G</math> would be a finite [[p-group|q-group]], hence [[Nilpotent group|nilpotent]], and therefore solvable.

Similarly, <math>G</math> cannot be abelian, otherwise it would be solvable. As <math>G</math> is simple, its center must therefore be trivial.

:* '''There is an element <math>g</math> of <math>G</math> which has <math>q^d</math> [[Conjugacy class|conjugates]], for some <math>d > 0</math>.'''

By the first statement of [[Sylow theorems|Sylow's theorem]], <math>G</math> has a [[subgroup]] <math>S</math> of order <math>p^a</math>. Because <math>S</math> is a nontrivial <math>p</math>-group, its center <math>Z(S)</math> is nontrivial. Fix a nontrivial element <math>g \in Z(S)</math>. The number of conjugates of <math>g</math> is equal to the index of its [[centralizer]] <math>G_g</math>, which divides the [[Index of a subgroup|index]] <math>q^b</math> of <math>S</math> (because <math>S</math> is a subgroup of <math>G_g</math>). Hence this number is of the form <math>q^d</math>. Moreover, the integer <math>d</math> is strictly positive, since <math>g</math> is nontrivial and therefore not central in <math>G</math>.

:* '''There exists a nontrivial [[irreducible representation]] <math>\rho</math> with [[Character theory|character]] <math>\chi</math>, such that its dimension <math>n</math> is not divisible by <math>q</math> and the [[complex number]] <math>\chi(g)</math> is not zero.'''

Let <math>(\chi_i)_{1 \leq i \leq h}</math> be the family of irreducible characters of <math>G</math> over <math>\mathbb{C}</math> (here <math>\chi_1</math> denotes the trivial character). Because <math>g</math> is not in the same conjugacy class as 1, the [[Schur orthogonality relations|orthogonality relation]] for the columns of the group's [[character table]] gives:

: <math>0=\sum_{i=1}^h \chi_i(1)\chi_i(g)= 1 + \sum_{i=2}^h \chi_i(1)\chi_i(g).</math>

Now the <math>\chi_i(g)</math> are [[algebraic integer]]s, because they are sums of [[Root of unity|roots of unity]]. If all the nontrivial irreducible characters which don't vanish at <math>g</math> take a value divisible by <math>q</math> at 1, we deduce that

: <math>-\frac1q=\sum_{i\ge 2,~\chi_i(g)\ne 0}\frac{\chi_i(1)}q\chi_i(g)</math>

is an algebraic integer (since it is a sum of integer multiples of algebraic integers), which is absurd. This proves the statement.

:* '''The complex number <math>q^d \chi(g) / n</math> is an algebraic integer.'''

The set of integer-valued [[Class function (algebra)|class functions]] on <math>G</math>, <math>Z(\Z[G])</math>, is a [[commutative ring]], [[Finitely generated module|finitely generated]] over <math>\Z</math>. All of its elements are thus integral over <math>\Z</math>, in particular the mapping <math>u</math> which takes the value 1 on the conjugacy class of <math>g</math> and 0 elsewhere.

The mapping <math>A\colon Z(\Z[G]) \rightarrow \operatorname{End}(\Complex^n)</math> which sends a class function <math>f</math> to

: <math>\sum_{s\in G} f(s)\rho(s)</math>

is a ring homomorphism. Because <math>\rho(s)^{-1} A(u) \rho(s) = A(u)</math> for all <math>s</math>, Schur's lemma implies that <math>A(u)</math> is a [[Homothetic transformation|homothety]] <math>\lambda I_n</math>. Its [[Trace (linear algebra)|trace]] <math>n \lambda</math> is equal to

: <math>\sum_{s\in G} f(s)\chi(s)=q^d\chi(g).</math>

Because the homothety <math>\lambda I_n</math> is the homomorphic image of an integral element, this proves that the complex number <math>\lambda = q^d \chi(g) / n</math> is an algebraic integer.

:* '''The complex number <math>\chi(g) / n</math> is an algebraic integer.'''

Since <math>q</math> is relatively prime to <math>n</math>, by [[Bézout's identity]] there are two integers <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> such that:

: <math>xq^d + yn=1\quad\text{therefore}\quad \frac{\chi(g)}{n}=x\frac{q^d\chi(g)}{n} + y\chi(g).</math>

Because a linear combination with integer coefficients of algebraic integers is again an algebraic integer, this proves the statement.

:* '''The image of <math>g</math>, under the representation <math>\rho</math>, is a homothety.'''

Let <math>\zeta</math> be the complex number <math>\chi(g) / n</math>. It is an algebraic integer, so its norm <math>N(\zeta)</math> (i.e. the product of its [[Conjugate element (field theory)|conjugates]], that is the roots of its [[Minimal polynomial (field theory)|minimal polynomial]] over <math>\Q</math>) is a nonzero integer. Now <math>\zeta</math> is the average of roots of unity (the eigenvalues of <math>\rho(g)</math>), hence so are its conjugates, so they all have an absolute value less than or equal to 1. Because the absolute value of their product <math>N(\zeta)</math> is greater than or equal to 1, their absolute value must all be 1, in particular <math>\zeta</math>, which means that the eigenvalues of <math>\rho(g)</math> are all equal, so <math>\rho(g)</math> is a homothety.

:* '''Conclusion'''
Let <math>N</math> be the kernel of <math>\rho</math>. The homothety <math>\rho(g)</math> is central in <math>\operatorname{Im}(\rho)</math> (which is canonically isomorphic to <math>G / N</math>), whereas <math>g</math> is not central in <math>G</math>. Consequently, the normal subgroup <math>N</math> of the simple group <math>G</math> is nontrivial, hence it is equal to <math>G</math>, which contradicts the fact that <math>\rho</math> is a nontrivial representation.

This contradiction proves the theorem.
